original_question: For incompressible fluid dynamics, especially at very large Reynolds number where viscosity is very small, is violent turbulence fundamentally caused by rough dependence on initial data rather than ordinary sensitive dependence on initial data? In this setting, rough dependence means that arbitrarily small perturbations of the initial condition can become substantial essentially instantly; for the Euler equations, at any nonzero time the solution map from initial data to the solution is continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere differentiable. Does this mechanism, or the very large derivative of the Navier-Stokes solution map in the high-Reynolds-number regime, explain why sufficiently large-Reynolds-number turbulence develops violently in short time?
target_in_paper: Section 3, the second major open problem, "Rough dependence on initial data - short term unpredictability (turbulence physics)," especially the conjectural claim that high-Reynolds-number violent turbulence is due to rough dependence on initial data rather than the sensitive dependence on initial data associated with chaos.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the paper's core target very well: it identifies the contrast between sensitive dependence on initial data and rough dependence on initial data; it correctly uses the 2D/3D Euler solution map as the motivating example, including the claim that for any nonzero time within the local-existence window the map is continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere differentiable; and it correctly includes the large-Reynolds-number Navier-Stokes heuristic that the derivative of the solution map becomes extremely large and may account for violent short-time turbulence.
missing_details: The paper presents this as the second major open problem in turbulence physics, under the heading "Rough dependence on initial data - short term unpredictability," not as an established theorem.

The fluid models in view are specifically the incompressible 2D or 3D Euler equations as the motivating zero-viscosity example, and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at large Reynolds number.
For Euler, the precise object is the time-t solution map sending an initial condition to the solution value at time t, for any t != 0 that is still small enough for local existence.

The paper explicitly separates two regimes: turbulence at not-large-enough Reynolds number may be due to sensitive dependence on initial data of chaos, while turbulence at large-enough Reynolds number may be due to rough dependence on initial data.
High Reynolds number is interpreted as sufficiently small viscosity, and the Euler equations correspond to the formal limit Re = infinity.

In this paper, the Navier-Stokes derivative-growth statement is heuristic/supporting context: the article says the derivative should be extremely large everywhere, with size indicated as approximately exp(C sqrt(t Re)) by citation to another work, rather than proving that bound here.
The term "short term unpredictability" is part of the official formulation and should be retained, because it is the paper's name for the proposed turbulence mechanism.
The introduction frames this as a turbulence-physics question, contrasted with turbulence engineering, which concerns effective statistical/averaged descriptions.
The paper does not specify a spatial domain, boundary conditions, or function spaces in this open-problem formulation; a faithful rewrite should not add extra settings not stated there.
There are no algebraic parameters such as ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree bounds, or nilpotency conditions relevant to this question.
refined_question: In the incompressible 2D/3D Euler-Navier-Stokes setting considered in the paper, is the correct turbulence-physics mechanism for sufficiently large Reynolds number (equivalently, sufficiently small viscosity) rough dependence on initial data - i.e. short term unpredictability - rather than the sensitive dependence on initial data of chaos? More precisely, given that for the Euler equations the time-t solution map from initial data to the solution at time t is, for every t != 0 within the local-existence interval, continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere differentiable, and given the paper's claim that for Navier-Stokes at large Reynolds number the derivative of the solution map should be extremely large everywhere because the Navier-Stokes map approaches the Euler map as Re -> infinity (heuristically of size about exp(C sqrt(t Re))), does this explain why high-Reynolds-number violent turbulence can develop substantial effects from arbitrarily small initial perturbations in very short time, whereas turbulence at not-large-enough Reynolds number may instead be due to ordinary chaotic sensitive dependence?
justification: This draft is targeting the paper's second major open problem, not a numbered theorem or proposition; in fact, this paper has no Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3. The abstract names the problem as rough dependence on initial data / short term unpredictability, the introduction classifies it as a turbulence-physics problem about the physical mechanism of turbulence, and Section 3 gives the actual conjectural formulation. Your draft is already close, but to be fully paper-faithful it should preserve the conjectural status, include the exact Euler time-t solution-map formulation with the local-existence caveat, keep the Reynolds-number contrast between chaos and rough dependence, and avoid presenting the Navier-Stokes derivative estimate as something proved inside this article.
